calls.head: The Golden Knights should drive the play
calls.body: The Golden Knights have been one of the league’s best at controlling the chances at 5-on-5, and the Canucks one of the worst. Expect the Golden Knights to spend more of the night in the Canucks’ end. That’s about the puck, not the scoreboard: goalies and finishing decide plenty of games the chances don’t.

surprises.head: Vegas picked Vancouver’s defense apart
surprises.body: Vancouver usually gives up some of the league’s most dangerous shots. Even by those standards, this was a night of good looks: Vegas’s shots at 5-on-5 had a 10.9% chance of scoring on the average shot, against their usual 6.4% (about 6.7% against Vancouver) and a league average of 6.3%. A team strays this far about once every 200 games. That’s rarer than once a season for any one team.

story.head: The Golden Knights edge the Canucks
paras: Paul Cotter struck first for the Canucks on the power play late in the first. It was a busy second period. Mitch Marner tied it up for Vegas midway through the period, and Victor Olofsson gave the Golden Knights the lead on the power play later in the period. Jonathan Lekkerimäki tied it up for Vancouver less than four minutes later. Marc Gatcomb scored his first goal for Vegas 34 seconds later to put the Golden Knights ahead for good. The Golden Knights didn’t get a shot on goal over the final 16 minutes, while the Canucks put nine on net.

The Golden Knights dominated, and the replays agree: run this game’s chances back a hundred times and the Golden Knights win about four in five. Adin Hill made 18 saves for the Golden Knights, and Kevin Lankinen, who gave up eight goals against Edmonton in his last start, kept the Canucks in it, stopping 25 of 28. The Knights improved to 2-1-0 and climbed to fifth in the Pacific, while the Canucks dropped to 2-2-0, slipping to sixth in the Pacific.

items.text: The Golden Knights have beaten the Canucks eight straight times, going back to the 2024-25 season.
Three of the preview’s four calls held.
